summary: Gives an applicability statement and scope for specifying RADIUS extensions to support Mobile IPv4. The goal is to allow RADIUS attributes that help Mobile IPv4 signaling. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A plan for how the sign-in system can help phones that move between networks.

questions: how does radius support mobile ip
what are radius extensions for mobile ip
subtitle: Framework for integrating Mobile IPv4 with existing sign-in systems.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv4 nodes need to securely bootstrap their configuration and establish security with home agents, but deploying this across networks requires standardized integration with existing AAA infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: The document specifies requirements for RADIUS attributes that allow Mobile IPv4 agents to interact with RADIUS servers during the registration and bootstrapping process, bridging Mobile IP signaling with AAA protocols.
tldr.outcome: Standardized RADIUS extensions enable consistent Mobile IPv4 support across wireless networks without requiring Diameter, maintaining backward compatibility with existing RADIUS deployments.

today: This is an informational RFC that defines the scope and requirements for RADIUS extensions to support Mobile IPv4. It has not been obsoleted or superseded and remains the baseline specification for adding Mobile IP support to RADIUS.

sections.title: Mobile IPv4 Bootstrapping Challenge
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 lets a phone keep its home address as it moves between networks. When a phone first connects, it must find a Home Agent and establish a secure relationship before any data can flow. This bootstrapping problem requires the phone to authenticate itself, but Mobile IPv4 does not define how to do this securely at scale.

Existing networks use RADIUS, a protocol for authentication and authorization that is proven and widely deployed. Connecting Mobile IPv4 to RADIUS would avoid building new infrastructure, but RADIUS predates Mobile IPv4 and lacks the attributes and procedures needed for Mobile IP signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone moving between networks needs permission to send data. The sign-in system already knows how to give permission, but it does not understand mobile phone requests yet.

sections.title: What RADIUS Extensions Are Needed
sections.content:
This RFC defines the scope of work: standardize new RADIUS attributes and specify how Mobile IPv4 agents (Home Agents and Foreign Agents) map between Mobile IP registration messages and RADIUS messages. The goal is to allow a RADIUS server to verify the authentication extensions that protect Mobile IPv4 registration and to distribute the security keys the agents need.

The extensions must be backward compatible with all existing RADIUS RFCs and must not extend the protocol with new message types, security mechanisms, or reliability guarantees. Instead, they reuse Diameter Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs) where possible to ensure consistency with other AAA protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan is to add new fields to RADIUS messages so it can understand mobile phone registration. Everything else stays the same.

sections.title: Goals and Non-Goals
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly lists what the extensions will and will not do. On the goal side, RADIUS servers must be able to understand and process Mobile IPv4 attributes, with backward compatibility with all existing RADIUS RFCs. Mobile IP agents must operate as RADIUS clients when translating between RADIUS and Mobile IP signaling.

On the non-goal side, the extensions will not create new RADIUS messages (unlike Diameter, which defined new commands for Mobile IP), will not extend RADIUS transport or reliability, and will not fully satisfy the Mobile IP Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting requirements from RFC 2977. Instead, the extensions focus on practical bootstrapping: providing attributes for configuration parameters and security keys during Mobile IPv4 registration.
sections.plainLanguage: The extensions have clear boundaries: they add knowledge to RADIUS but do not change how it fundamentally works. They help bootstrap mobile phones but do not redesign RADIUS.

sections.title: Security Tensions and Limitations
sections.content:
The document recognizes a fundamental tension: Mobile IPv4 security requires end-to-end trust between the phone and the Home Agent, but RADIUS uses hop-by-hop security with intermediate proxies that must be trusted. This conflicts with guidelines for key management that limit key scope to only parties that need the key.

The document states that enhancing RADIUS security itself is a non-goal. Instead, the RADIUS extensions must use existing security procedures like Message-Authenticator and rely on IPsec when stronger protection is needed. Future work on RADIUS crypto-agility and key wrapping may improve the situation, but for now, deployments must trust their RADIUS intermediaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Security is tricky: the phone needs to trust only its home network, but RADIUS passes messages through middle servers that must also be trusted. The document accepts this limitation.
